prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff ERISA participant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plan administrator's decision is arbitrary and capricious when it relies on a file-only review and disregards treating physicians without explanation.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**The denial is arbitrary and capricious because it rests on a file-only review that disregards Plaintiff's treating physicians without explanation.**

This Court reviews the district court's ERISA judgment de novo, applying the same standard that governed below. *Glenn v. MetLife*, 461 F.3d 660, 665–66 (6th Cir. 2006), *aff'd sub nom. Metro. Life Ins. Co. v. Glenn*, 554 U.S. 105 (2008). Where the plan confers discretion, a denial survives only "if it is the result of a deliberate, principled reasoning process and if it is supported by substantial evidence." *Elliott v. Metro. Life Ins. Co.*, 473 F.3d 613, 617 (6th Cir. 2006) (citation and internal quotation marks omitted). Review is deferential, but "deferential review is not no review, and deference need not be abject." *McDonald v. W.-S. Life Ins. Co.*, 347 F.3d 161, 172 (6th Cir. 2003) (citation and internal quotation marks omitted). Any conflict of interest arising because the administrator both decides and pays claims is also a factor. *Glenn*, 554 U.S. at 112, 117.

**A. An administrator may not set aside treating-physician evidence without a reasoned basis.**

Treating physicians receive no automatic deference, and ERISA imposes no discrete burden of explanation when an administrator credits reliable conflicting evidence. *Black & Decker Disability Plan v. Nord*, 538 U.S. 822, 834 (2003). But administrators "may not arbitrarily refuse to credit a claimant's reliable evidence, including the opinions of a treating physician." *Id.* A denial that never confronts that evidence, or dismisses it without reasons, reflects no principled choice between competing opinions. *See Elliott*, 473 F.3d at 620–21; *Evans v. UnumProvident Corp.*, 434 F.3d 866, 877–80 (6th Cir. 2006) (affirming judgment for the claimant where the administrator's contrary evidence, including a file review, did not adequately answer the treating physician).

**B. Reliance on a file-only review heightens the defect.**

A file review is not improper in itself. But the failure to conduct a physical examination, particularly where the plan reserves the right to do so, "may, in some cases, raise questions about the thoroughness and accuracy of the benefits determination." *Calvert v. Firstar Fin., Inc.*, 409 F.3d 286, 295 (6th Cir. 2005). *Calvert* rejected a reviewer's conclusions that failed to grapple with contrary evidence in the record. *Id.* at 296–97.

This Court has repeatedly set aside denials resting on such reviews. *See Kalish v. Liberty Mut./Liberty Life Assurance Co. of Bos.*, 419 F.3d 501, 508–11 (6th Cir. 2005) (reviewer failed to rebut the treating physician's contrary conclusions); *Bennett v. Kemper Nat'l Servs., Inc.*, 514 F.3d 547, 554–56 (6th Cir. 2008) (reviews failed to address significant contrary evidence); *Helfman v. GE Grp. Life Assurance Co.*, 573 F.3d 383, 393–96 (6th Cir. 2009) (denial lacked a reasoned treatment of the claimant's medical evidence). Scrutiny is especially warranted when a non-examining reviewer discounts the claimant's reported symptoms. *Shaw v. AT&T Umbrella Benefit Plan No. 1*, 795 F.3d 538, 548–51 (6th Cir. 2015) (denial arbitrary where the administrator, among other errors, disregarded treating-source evidence and relied on file reviewers who questioned the claimant's complaints without examining [him/her]).

**C. This denial fails that standard.**

[Plaintiff's] treating physicians, [names], documented [diagnoses, objective findings, and restrictions] and concluded that [Plaintiff] [plan definition of disability]. [Record citations.] The Administrator instead relied on [reviewer], who never examined [Plaintiff], although the plan [reserves the right to require an examination]. [Record citations.] Neither the reviewer nor the denial letter explained why [specific findings] were unreliable or insufficient. [Record citations.]

That omission is not cured by reciting that the records were "reviewed." Listing evidence is not weighing it. Nor may counsel supply in litigation a rationale the Administrator never gave. The question is whether the Administrator's own process was deliberate and principled. On this record, it was not. The Court should reverse and order benefits awarded or, at minimum, remand to the Administrator for a full and fair review that meaningfully addresses the treating physicians' evidence. *See Elliott*, 473 F.3d at 621–23.
